content: This is an updated version of the original Cochrane review published in 2012. Epilepsy is one of the most prevalent chronic neurological disorders. Despite the availability of numerous antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), approximately 30% of individuals with epilepsy continue to experience seizures. For this group, more aggressive treatment strategies are required, as monotherapy—the preferred initial treatment approach—often fails to achieve seizure control. However, polytherapy, which involves the use of multiple AEDs, frequently leads to undesirable side effects. These include neurological issues such as somnolence, ataxia, and dizziness; psychiatric and behavioral symptoms; and metabolic disturbances, such as osteoporosis or alterations in hepatic enzyme activity. Therefore, there is an urgent need for AEDs that are better tolerated, particularly for this subset of patients. Some reports have suggested that melatonin may have antiepileptic properties and a favorable safety profile. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of melatonin as an add-on treatment for epilepsy. For the most recent update, a comprehensive search was conducted in several databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group's Specialized Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and MEDLINE, with the last searches performed in January 2016. Additional references were identified by reviewing bibliographies of relevant studies, handsearching selected journals and conference proceedings, and contacting melatonin manufacturers and original investigators to uncover any unpublished studies. No language restrictions were applied. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), whether double-blind, single-blind, or unblinded, as well as parallel-group or cross-over studies. Participants included individuals with epilepsy of any age or gender, including children and adults with disabilities. The intervention involved the administration of melatonin as an add-on treatment to any AED(s), compared to either an add-on placebo or no additional treatment. The review authors independently selected studies for inclusion based on predefined criteria, extracted relevant data, and assessed the methodological quality of the trials. The outcomes evaluated included a reduction in seizure frequency by at least 50%, complete seizure freedom, adverse events, and quality of life. Six studies, involving a total of 125 participants (106 of whom were under 18 years of age), were included in the review. Two types of comparisons were analyzed: melatonin versus placebo, and melatonin 5 mg versus melatonin 10 mg. Due to insufficient data on the outcomes of interest, meta-analyses could not be performed, and the findings were summarized narratively. Four of the studies were randomized, double-blind, cross-over, placebo-controlled trials, while the remaining two were randomized, double-blind, parallel, placebo-controlled trials. Only two studies provided specific data on seizure frequency during the trial compared to baseline. In these studies, no participants experienced a change in seizure frequency during the trial compared to their baseline seizure frequency. Two studies systematically assessed adverse effects, with one reporting a worsening of headache in a child with migraine who was receiving melatonin treatment. Only one study systematically evaluated quality of life, and it found no statistically significant improvement in quality of life in the group receiving add-on melatonin. The authors concluded that the included studies were of poor methodological quality and did not systematically evaluate seizure frequency or adverse events. As a result, it was not possible to perform a meta-analysis or draw definitive conclusions about the role of melatonin in reducing seizure frequency or improving quality of life in individuals with epilepsy.
